summary: This unit teaches you to promote a business: to set measurable promotional aims, define the target audience and a clear honest message, choose the promotional mix and digital channels, set a budget and compare media, promote lawfully and ethically, brief staff, and measure results so that you can keep, change or stop each activity.

blocks.p: Promotion is how a business tells the right people about what it offers and persuades them to act. This unit teaches you to plan promotion that fits the business's aims and budget, choose the right activities and media, keep promotion honest and lawful, brief staff, and measure results so that money is spent where it works. It is for managers in small and medium Jamaican businesses, hotels, schools and public bodies who run or oversee promotion, whether or not they have a marketing department.

blocks.h: What you must be able to do

head: Task
What it means in practice
rows: Write clear, measurable aims linked to the business's goals
Describe the target customers and write one clear message that sets the business apart
Select advertising, sales promotion, public relations, personal selling, direct, digital and other activities that suit the audience and the budget
Run a website, listings, social media and email so that they are consistent, current and lawful
Set a promotion budget by a sound method, compare media costs and plan timing
Avoid misleading claims, respect copyright and customers' data, and think about ethics
Write a promotion plan and prepare staff so that they can explain the offer
Track results with simple measures and decide what to keep, change or stop

blocks.note: Money for promotion is limited. The skill is not in spending more but in spending where the right people will see the message and act on it, and in knowing what each activity achieved.
blocks.label: Remember

blocks.p: Marketing is the whole task of understanding customers and offering them what they value. It is often described through the **four Ps**: product, price, place and promotion. Promotion is the P that communicates the other three. Promotion cannot rescue a poor product or a wrong price; it works best when the offer is good and the customers know about it.
AIDA describes the stages that a promotion takes a customer through.

flow: Interest: the customer wants to know more
Desire: the customer wants the product
Action: the customer enquires, visits or buys

blocks.p: A good advert, flyer or web page makes it easy to move from one stage to the next, and ends with a clear action: 'Call 876-555-0100', 'Order today', 'Visit us on Hope Road'.
Before any activity, state what the promotion is to achieve. A good aim is **SMART**: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.

head: Weak aim
SMART aim
rows: Raise the number of enquiries about wedding cakes from 20 to 30 a month by the end of March
Raise the number of people in Savanna-la-Mar who say they have heard of the shop from 25% to 40% in six months
Sell more of the new sauce
Sell 600 bottles of the new sauce in three months in the 10 supermarkets we supply

blocks.p: Typical promotional aims: **inform** (a new product), **persuade** (choose us), **remind** (customers who already know us), **build a brand**, **win leads**, **clear stock**, **build loyalty**.

blocks.h: Know your market and your competitors

ul: Who buys, how often, and why do they choose a business like ours?
What do competitors offer and say? Where do they advertise?
What season, event or trend affects demand?
What are our strengths: price, quality, location, service, speed, local ingredients?

blocks.p: A quick SWOT (strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats) of the business and of its competitors helps you find what to say.

blocks.h: Positioning and the unique selling point

blocks.p: A **unique selling point (USP)** is the clear benefit that sets the business apart from its competitors, such as 'delivery in the same day', 'fresh fish from our own boats', 'repairs guaranteed for a year'. **Positioning** is the place the business takes in the customer's mind. A business that competes only on price invites a price war that nobody wins. Stress something customers value that rivals cannot easily copy.

Promotion works when it is aimed at **a defined group** rather than everyone. Describe the group by who they are (age, work, income, family), where they are, what they need, what media they use and when they buy. Businesses often have more than one audience.

head: Business
Audiences
What changes between them
rows: Supermarket buyers; tourists buying gifts; households
Trade buyers want margin, supply and shelf-life; tourists want story and gift packaging; households want taste and price
Different times, fees and media for each
Overseas visitors; Jamaican residents; tour agents

blocks.note: A promotion aimed at everyone usually reaches no one well. Choose the audience first, then the message and the media.
blocks.label: Tip

blocks.p: The key message is the one thing you most want the audience to remember. It should be **clear, true, short, about a benefit to the customer** and the same wherever the customer meets it.

head: Weak
Better
rows: A flyer listing 14 tours in small print, with no headline
One headline: 'Blue Mountain day tour, hotel pick-up, J$9,500'
'Made from scotch bonnet peppers grown on three Manchester farms'
'Your car back the same day, or your next oil change is free'

blocks.p: A brand is the name, logo, colours, tone and promise that customers link with the business. When the radio advert, shop sign, website and social pages all use the same name, logo, colours and slogan, customers recognise the business and trust it. When they differ, customers may not know that they belong to the same business, and the money spent on each is wasted. Write a short brand guide (logo files, two or three colours, fonts, slogan, tone of voice) and give it to everyone who produces material.

Do not promote what you cannot supply. If an advert brings 200 orders and the business can make 80, the extra customers are disappointed and tell others. Check stock, staff and delivery capacity before launching.

The **promotional mix** is the set of tools used to communicate with customers: **advertising, sales promotion, public relations, personal selling and direct marketing**. Digital marketing and social media are now part of nearly every element. Choose the mix by audience, aim, product and budget.

head: Tool
What it is
Strengths
Limits
Example
rows: Radio spot, newspaper advert, bus-shelter poster
Fast results; good for clearing stock
Can train customers to wait for deals; cuts margin
Buy one get one free; coupons; free sample
Earning favourable attention without paying for space
Press release about a gift to a children's home; open day
Paying to be linked with an event or team
A parish netball league, a school sports day
Answers questions; builds relationships; best for costly, complex or made-to-order products
A sales representative visiting a hotel kitchen
Displays and offers where customers choose and pay
Limited to people already in the shop
Counter display, shelf talker, till-point offers
A stand at a business expo
A stand at a national expo
A reward for clients who bring a friend

head: Situation
Likely choice
rows: Everyday product to the general public
Advertising, POS, sales promotion, social media
A new business to local residents
Word of mouth, community talks, social media, flyers
A business selling to other businesses
Networking, trade shows, direct contact, short free talks
Slow-selling stock near its expiry date

blocks.p: PR builds a good name through **news, community work and relationships**, not paid space. A **press release** is a short, factual news story that the business sends to the media about itself (a new product, an award, a gift to a school). Give the who, what, when, where and why in the first paragraph, add a quote and a contact. Other PR: open days, school talks, community clean-ups, sponsoring local events, supporting charities, and answering the media honestly.

**Risks to manage:** PR cannot be controlled, so a story may not be used; community involvement must be genuine, because it looks false if done only for publicity; a complaint or accident can become bad news, so prepare a short statement and a person who speaks for the business; do not promise more than you deliver.

blocks.h: Promoting to businesses and to the public

head: Point
Selling to the public (consumers)
Selling to other businesses (B2B)
rows: Few; decide slowly, often a group; need quotations and references
Advertising, social media, offers, point of sale, word of mouth
Personal selling, networking, trade shows, direct contact, short free talks, case studies
Reliability, savings, support, proof of results
A juice bar with flyers and social media posts
An accounting firm giving short talks at a business group in May Pen

blocks.h: Traditional and digital media in rural Jamaica

head: Medium
Strengths
Limits
rows: Wide reach, including areas with weak internet; trusted local stations; works for spoken messages
Short message; cost per spot; people cannot look back at it
Credible; good for detailed offers and notices
Constant presence in a place; good for location and brand
Brief message; fixed place; cost of space
Community channels (churches, markets, clubs, notice boards, vans)
Cheap; trusted; reaches the exact area
Low cost, targeted, easy to measure and reply
Needs data and phones; some customers are not online
Customers find you when they look for you
Needs upkeep; needs to be found

blocks.p: A good rural mix often combines a trusted local radio station, signs at the business, community word of mouth and a free social media page or messaging number, with the share between them set by where the customers are.

ul: **SEO (search engine optimisation)** is the work of helping a website appear higher in internet search results, by using clear titles, words customers search for, useful pages, mobile-friendly design and an accurate business listing.
**Cost per click (CPC)** is the amount a business pays each time someone clicks on its online advert. Total cost = clicks × cost per click.
**Opt-in** means a person actively agrees, for example by ticking a box, to receive messages. Opt-in lists are the safe basis for email and text promotion.
A **focus group** is a small group of target customers brought together to discuss a planned advert or product before it is launched, so that mistakes are found early.
**Brand identity** is the look of the business (logo, colours, typefaces) used in the same way everywhere.

blocks.p: Discounts boost sales quickly but can harm a business if used too often. Customers learn to wait for the sale, begin to see the brand as cheap, and profit per sale falls. Use offers with an end date and a purpose: clearing stock, introducing a product, or rewarding loyal customers.

**Keeping a customer usually costs less than winning a new one.** Existing customers already know the business, so a share of the budget should go to reminders, loyalty rewards, thank-you messages and referral offers. A loyalty card, when used lawfully, also shows what customers buy, which helps to plan future offers.

blocks.h: Trade shows: from preparation to follow-up

flow: Set aims (leads, orders, contacts) and a budget for the stand, travel, samples and staff
Choose the right show: is your target audience there?
Design the stand and materials; prepare samples and an offer for the show
Train staff to greet visitors, explain the offer and collect contact details
At the show: record every lead, with what they want
Follow up within days with a message or call
Count leads, orders and cost; review and decide whether to attend next time

blocks.p: Involve staff before, during and after: explain the aims and the offer; ask for ideas (staff often know what customers ask); give them product knowledge, scripts for questions and the right to apply the offer; reward good referrals; and share the results. Staff who understand a promotion explain it better and feel part of the business. Customers ask the people they meet: cashiers, drivers, receptionists. Brief them before every promotion so that they can explain the offer, its dates and conditions, and answer questions. A good advert followed by a staff member who says 'I don't know about that' wastes the money.

blocks.note: Jamaican businesses often get their best new customers by word of mouth. A good service, a fair price and an easy way to recommend you (a referral reward, a shareable post) are among the cheapest forms of promotion.
blocks.label: Jamaica

blocks.p: Many customers look for a business online before they visit, including on a phone. A business that cannot be found online may lose customers it never knew about.

head: Tool
What to do
rows: Business listing on maps and search sites
Claim the listing and keep the name, address, phone, hours and photos accurate; ask for reviews
Make it easy to see what you offer, how to contact you and how to buy or book; make it work on a phone; keep prices and hours current
Choose the platforms your customers use; post regularly; reply to messages and comments quickly
A business number customers can message; set clear opening hours for replies
Send useful offers to people who have agreed to receive them

blocks.h: Setting up social media for a guest house

ol: Decide the aim (for example, more direct bookings from overseas and from Jamaican residents).
Choose one or two platforms where guests are, and use the same name, logo and colours.
Fill the profile: place, contact number, booking link, hours and photos.
Plan a calendar: rooms, breakfast, sunsets, local walks, guest stories, offers.
Reply to messages and comments the same day.
Ask guests to tag the guest house and to review it.
Track followers, enquiries, bookings and which posts work best.

ul: Use a **content calendar** to plan posts ahead, so that they are regular, timely and on message (for example around Easter, Emancipation and Independence, back-to-school and Christmas).
Mix useful, entertaining and selling posts. Pictures and short videos usually get more attention than text.
Reply to comments and questions promptly and politely.
Paid adverts on social media can be aimed by age, place and interest, and start from small budgets. Test two versions and keep the better one.
Use only photos, music and text the business owns or has permission to use.

blocks.p: An influencer is a person with an audience who recommends products. Choose one whose **followers match your target customers**, who has a record of honest posts, and agree in writing what will be posted and when. **Paid or sponsored posts must be clearly shown as such**, and free gifts or stays must also be disclosed. Claims in the posts must be true.

ul: Ask every customer for an honest review, for example with a link or a QR code at checkout or on the receipt.
Never write fake reviews or pay for them, and do not ask friends to post praise they did not earn: it is dishonest and can break consumer rules.
Answer every review, good and bad. For a harsh review that is partly true, **reply politely, thank the customer, fix the issue and say so**.
Learn from patterns in reviews: they are free market research.

blocks.h: Direct messages, email and data protection

blocks.p: Customers' phone numbers, emails and addresses are personal data. In line with the **data protection law**, a business should:

ul: collect only the data it needs and say what it will be used for;
send promotional messages only to people who have agreed;
make it easy to opt out, and remove people who do;
keep the data secure, and keep it only as long as it is needed;
never buy lists of phone numbers from people who have not been given the customers' permission.

blocks.note: A message that people did not ask for makes them angry and may break the data protection law. A small list of people who want to hear from you is worth more than a large list that does not.
blocks.label: Remember

head: Method
How it works
Weakness
rows: A set share of last year's or expected sales. Example: 2.5% of J$36,000,000 = J$900,000
Cuts the budget when sales fall, just when promotion is needed; ignores what must be achieved
What is left after other costs
Treats promotion as a spare, not an investment
Set the aims, list the activities needed to reach them, cost each, and add them up
Needs careful planning, but links money to results

blocks.p: The objective-and-task method is the best starting point because it starts from the aims. Where the total is more than the money available, reduce the aims or choose cheaper tasks.
Aim: win 40 corporate Christmas-party bookings by 15 December. Budget available J$600,000.

head: Task
Cost (J$)
rows: Social media adverts for six weeks

blocks.p: Always include a **contingency** (often 5% to 10%) for unexpected costs and keep a record of every cost so that you can measure results. Work each sum twice.
Terms used in media planning:

head: Term
Meaning
rows: The number of different people who see or hear the message
The average number of times each person sees or hears it
Cost ÷ reach × 1,000. It compares media of different sizes

blocks.p: Station B is cheaper for each thousand people reached. But a low cost per thousand is useful only if the audience includes your target customers: a cheaper audience that does not buy is not a bargain. Also consider frequency: one exposure is rarely enough.

blocks.h: Where to spend: value for money

ul: Choose media your target group really uses (hotel desks and review sites for tourists; church and community groups for older people; social media for young adults; trade groups for business customers).
Targeted, low-cost activities (social adverts, offers to past customers) often give better value than general ones for a small budget.
Spend most where results are best, and test small before spending big.

blocks.p: Time promotions to when customers decide. Examples: school uniforms and books in the weeks before the new school year in September; hotels and tour operators before the winter and summer peaks; gifts and food before Christmas; businesses that sell to other firms ahead of their budget and booking cycles (for corporate Christmas events, usually well before December). Allow time to plan, produce and book media: a good promotion starts weeks before the sales peak.

When a rival starts a large price promotion, do not copy it at once. First **assess the effect on your sales** and look at your own strengths. You may prefer to stress quality or service, or to offer a targeted reward to your best customers.

head: Issue
What to do
rows: Only state what you can prove. If tests show a product removes most but not all germs, do not say 'removes 100%'. Keep the evidence.
Show the real price, the conditions and the dates; do not advertise stock you do not have
Compare fairly with facts you can prove; do not insult competitors
A photo, song, logo or text belongs to its owner. Get permission or a licence, or use material you own or that is free to use
Follow the data protection law as above
Say clearly when posts or reviews are paid for or sponsored
Think carefully about the ethics, and any rules, before aiming promotions for sugary or unhealthy products at children
Be especially careful: a false claim can harm people and brings legal and reputational damage

blocks.p: Jamaica has consumer protection and fair competition laws, rules about broadcasting and advertising, and laws on copyright. A manager should know the **purpose** of these laws and check with the legal adviser, the trade association or the regulator when unsure. Do not guess.

blocks.note: Ethics means asking 'is it right?' as well as 'is it allowed?'. A promotion that tricks customers may win a sale today and lose the customer and the reputation for ever.
blocks.label: Remember

sections.title: Planning, running and measuring a promotion

blocks.p: A promotion plan is a short document that answers these questions.

head: Part
Question answered
rows: What are we trying to achieve, by when?
Who are we trying to reach?
What is the one thing they should remember?
What will we do, where and why?
What will each activity cost, with a contingency?
What happens when? Who does it?
How will we know if it worked? What targets?

flow: Define the audience and the message
Set the budget and the timetable
Run the promotion and track results

blocks.p: Measure each activity, not only the whole campaign. Work out each figure and check it twice.

head: Measure
Formula
Example
rows: Return on promotion, a second example
Likes, comments and shares ÷ people reached × 100

blocks.p: **Use gross profit, not sales**, to judge return. A promotion that raises sales by giving deep discounts can raise sales and still lower profit, so always check the margin.

Ask customers 'How did you hear about us?', and give each advert its own code, link, telephone number or coupon. Then you can count the customers each one brought. To measure awareness, **survey target customers before and after** the campaign and compare.

blocks.h: What the numbers do not show

ul: Some activities (a sponsorship, a radio campaign) build awareness that leads to sales later or through other channels.
Sales also move with the season, the weather and competitors' actions.
A short campaign may not have had time to work.
Customers may not remember how they heard of you.

blocks.p: Use the numbers with judgement. When one channel gives a much better return, move more of the budget there, but check that results hold at the higher spend.

After the campaign, list what worked and did not, with figures, and file the review. If sales rose but profit fell, look first at whether **discounts and costs cut too deeply into the margin**. Use the lessons to write the next plan.

ul: explain the role of promotion in the marketing plan and use the AIDA model.
write SMART promotional aims.
describe a target audience and write a clear, true key message and USP.
keep the brand consistent across all materials.
name the elements of the promotional mix and choose the best for a given business and audience.
use a website, listings, social media, influencers and reviews well, and follow the data protection law for messages.
set a promotion budget by the objective-and-task method, including a contingency, and explain the weaknesses of the other methods.
compare media by reach, frequency and cost per thousand.
time promotions to the customers' buying seasons.
promote honestly, respect copyright and think about ethics.
write a promotion plan and brief front-line staff.
work out cost per enquiry, conversion rate, return, engagement rate and redemption rate, and use them to decide what to do next.

terms: Communicating with customers to inform and persuade them.
The set of tools used to promote: advertising, sales promotion, PR, personal selling and direct marketing.
Unique selling point: the benefit that sets a business apart.
The group of customers a promotion is aimed at.
The name, look and promise customers link with a business.
A short-term offer to boost sales.
Earning favourable attention without paying for advertising.
The number of different people who see a message.
How many times, on average, each person sees a message.
The share of enquiries that become customers.
Extra gross profit less cost, as a percentage of cost.
An amount set aside for unexpected costs.
Setting a budget by costing the activities needed to reach the aims.

c1.title: A pepper sauce producer in Mandeville
c1.text: Marcia Reid makes a scotch bonnet pepper sauce in Mandeville from peppers bought from three local farms. She sells to 12 supermarkets and, increasingly, to tourists who buy it as a gift. Yearly sales are J$30,000,000. She wants to launch a new gift-pack and has asked what to say, to whom, and how much to spend. Her sales have fallen for two months because of a poor pepper harvest.

c2.title: A computer training centre in Montego Bay
c2.text: A private computer training centre in Montego Bay runs evening classes for working adults aged 25 to 45. Its website works badly on a phone, although most enquirers use phones. The manager has been offered a list of 5,000 mobile phone numbers by a stranger. Last week the centre's post about a free open evening reached 12,500 people and got 500 likes, comments and shares.

c3.title: A guest house in Falmouth
c3.text: Dorrett Campbell owns a six-room guest house in Falmouth that serves a Jamaican breakfast and offers guided walks of the old town. Competitors are cutting room prices. A friend suggests she ask relatives to write five-star reviews, and a travel blogger has offered to post about the guest house in return for a free weekend. Dorrett has not yet asked guests at checkout for reviews.

c4.title: Results of a catering campaign at a Portmore bakery
c4.text: A bakery in Portmore ran three promotions last quarter to win catering orders. Radio cost J$120,000 and brought 48 enquiries, 6 orders and J$210,000 gross profit. Flyers cost J$40,000 and brought 25 enquiries, 5 orders and J$95,000 gross profit. Social media adverts cost J$60,000 and brought 120 enquiries, 9 orders and J$180,000 gross profit.

c5.title: A Christmas promotion by an events company
c5.text: An events company in Kingston wants 40 corporate Christmas party bookings by 15 December. It has J$600,000. Two radio stations offered advertising: Station A charges J$96,000 for a week and reaches 160,000 listeners; Station B charges J$150,000 and reaches 300,000. The planned costs of other tasks are brochures J$85,000, a stand at a business expo J$250,000 and six weeks of social adverts J$140,000. The Chamber of Commerce has also asked for J$100,000 to sponsor its awards dinner.

questions.q: Which is the best promotional aim for the new gift-pack?
o: Make the gift-pack well known across the whole of Jamaica as soon as she can
Sell more sauce than last year in every supermarket that she supplies now
Sell 800 gift-packs through five tourist shops in four months
Get tourists to like the gift-pack and to tell their friends about it later
questions.why: A good aim is specific, measurable and has a time limit. The first option states a number, the outlets and the period, so that results can be checked.

questions.q: Marcia's customers include supermarket buyers and tourists. What is the best approach to the message?
o: Use different messages and channels for each group, based on what each values
Use one message for both groups so that it is simple for everyone to remember
Aim only at tourists, since supermarkets do not buy gift-packs from her
Show the lowest price in all her promotion so that every group is attracted
questions.why: Different audiences value different things: trade buyers look at margin, supply and shelf-life, and tourists look at story and gift appeal. One message rarely suits both.

questions.q: Which claim is the best for the key message on the gift-pack?
o: The hottest and best-tasting pepper sauce anywhere in the whole world
Healthier for every customer than all other pepper sauces on sale today
The cheapest gift that a visitor will find anywhere in the whole of Jamaica
Made from scotch bonnet peppers grown on three Manchester farms
questions.why: A good message is clear, true and about a benefit. The origin of the peppers can be proved and is a feature competitors cannot easily copy. The others are claims she could not support.

questions.q: Marcia thinks of setting her budget at 4% of sales, which is J$1,200,000. What is the main weakness of this method now?
o: The percentage is too small to pay for any worthwhile promotion at all
Her budget will fall as sales have fallen, just when promotion is needed
It is not possible to work out a percentage of a figure for a whole year
Percentage budgets are only suitable for very large companies with agencies
questions.why: A percentage of sales ties the budget to past sales rather than to what must be achieved, so the budget shrinks when sales fall. Starting from the aims and costing the tasks is better.

questions.q: The manager is offered a list of 5,000 mobile phone numbers by a stranger. What should he do?
o: Accept and send one message only, to keep within the data protection law
Decline, as those people have not agreed to receive messages from the centre
Accept, but send only to the numbers that begin with the 876 area code
Accept the list if the stranger gives his word that the numbers are real
questions.why: Promotional messages should go only to people who have agreed to hear from the business. Numbers bought from a stranger carry no such permission and may breach the data protection law.

questions.q: The centre's open-evening post was seen by 12,500 people, and 500 of them liked, commented on or shared it. Work out the engagement rate.
questions.why: 500 ÷ 12,500 × 100 = 4%. The rate compares the response with the number of people reached.

questions.q: Most enquirers use phones, but the website works badly on them. What is the most useful change?
o: Make the courses and fees clear, with an easy enrol button for phones
Add more photographs of the building and its classrooms to the home page
Put a long history of the centre and its founders on the first page
Remove the fees from the site so that people have to call to find them out
questions.why: The website must work for the way customers use it. A phone-friendly page with fees and a clear next step makes it easy to move from interest to action.

questions.q: The centre wants to advertise its evening classes on social media. Which targeting is best?
o: All users in Jamaica of every age, shown at any time of the day or night
Only the people who already follow the centre's page on social media
Adults aged 25 to 45 in St James, shown at night, with two versions tested
School children and their parents, since they are online for most of the day
questions.why: Targeting by age, place and time fits the target group and avoids wasted spend. Testing two versions shows which works better.

questions.q: A friend suggests that Dorrett's relatives write five-star reviews. What should she do?
o: Accept, but ask each relative to add photographs of their visit
Accept, but ask them to give only three or four stars so it looks real
Refuse, and ask real guests to give honest reviews
Accept if every relative has stayed at the guest house at least once
questions.why: Fake or unearned reviews mislead customers, damage trust if found out and may break consumer rules. Honest reviews from real guests are worth more.

questions.q: Which is the best choice of influencer for the guest house?
o: A blogger whose followers are likely guests and who will disclose the free stay
The entertainer with the most followers, whatever those followers are interested in
A local person who promises to post about the guest house as often as possible
Any blogger who will agree to post without asking for anything in return
questions.why: The influencer's followers should match the target guests, the arrangement should be agreed in writing, and a free stay must be disclosed in the posts.

questions.q: Competitors are cutting prices. What should Dorrett stress in her promotion?
o: The same price cuts as the others, so that the guest house is not left behind
That the competitors are less honest with their guests than she is
Nothing at all, until the price war between the guest houses has ended
What makes her guest house different, such as the breakfast and local walks
questions.why: Competing only on price starts a price war. Stressing benefits that customers value and rivals cannot easily copy protects the margin.

questions.q: Which action best brings in genuine reviews for the guest house?
o: Ask for reviews only from guests who say that they enjoyed their stay
Ask each guest at checkout and give a link or QR code to the review page
Offer a free night to the guest who writes the best review of the year
Post a request on the page and wait for guests to notice it online
questions.why: Asking every guest at the moment of checkout, with an easy link, gets honest and more numerous reviews. Asking only happy guests or offering prizes can skew the record.

questions.q: What was the cost per enquiry for the social media adverts?
questions.why: Cost ÷ enquiries = J$60,000 ÷ 120 = J$500.

questions.q: What was the conversion rate of the radio advert from enquiries to orders?
questions.why: Orders ÷ enquiries × 100 = 6 ÷ 48 × 100 = 12.5%.

questions.q: Return = (gross profit minus cost) ÷ cost × 100. Which channel gave the best return?
o: Social media adverts, at 200%
Flyers, at 137.5%
Radio, at 75%
All three gave the same return

questions.q: What is the best use of these results when planning next quarter?
o: Move all of the budget to social media at once, since it did best
Keep the same split, because every channel made a profit for the bakery
Move some radio money to social media, then check the return holds
Stop the flyers at once, because they cost the least of the three
questions.why: Moving money to the stronger channel makes sense, but returns may fall as spending rises, and radio may build awareness that the figures do not show. Test the change in steps.

questions.q: Using the objective-and-task method, add a 10% contingency to brochures, the expo stand and social adverts. How much of the J$600,000 is left unallocated?
questions.why: Tasks total 85,000 + 250,000 + 140,000 = J$475,000. A 10% contingency is J$47,500, so J$522,500 is planned and J$77,500 remains.

questions.q: Which radio station is the better buy, and why?
o: Station B, as it costs less per thousand, if its listeners are buyers
Station A, because it costs less in total for the week of advertising
Station B, because a bigger reach always brings in more bookings
Station A, because a smaller audience is easier to persuade
questions.why: Cost per thousand is J$600 for A and J$500 for B, so B is cheaper per person reached. The saving matters only if the listeners are people who book corporate events.

questions.q: When should the company start promoting its Christmas party packages?
o: In the first week of December, when Christmas is on everyone's mind
On 15 December, which is the booking deadline for the whole campaign
After the New Year, so that it is ready for the next Christmas season
In September or October, as companies book well ahead
questions.why: Business customers plan and book ahead. Promotion must start early enough to produce material, book media and reach them before they decide.

questions.q: The Chamber of Commerce asks for J$100,000 to sponsor its awards dinner. What should the company check first?
o: Whether the chamber is a long-established and well-known organisation
Whether its audience matches the target clients and what the sponsor gets
Whether the amount can be found within the unallocated budget left over
Whether competitors have sponsored the dinner in earlier years or not
questions.why: A sponsorship is worth what the right audience and the benefits (logo, speaking, contacts) deliver for the money. Fit with the target customers is the first test.
